name: Ethylhexyl triazone
lead: Ethylhexyl triazone (octyl triazone, EHT; Uvinul T 150 from BASF, Parsol EHT from DSM-Firmenich) is an oil-soluble organic UVB filter with an absorption maximum near 314 nm. Its structure is a triazine ring bearing three 2-ethylhexyl benzoate groups.[1][2]

For appearance, sunscreen filters matter because ultraviolet exposure is a major driver of visible skin aging, uneven pigmentation and tanning. A UVB filter such as EHT contributes to the SPF of a product, so it supports the routine of daily sun protection that people use to keep skin tone even and delay lines and spots; its role is as one ingredient within a multi-filter formula [2].

Grokipedia describes it as highly photostable and used at low concentrations to raise SPF, and says it is permitted in the EU at up to 5% but lacks US approval as a sunscreen active.[2] Its Wikipedia article is a short stub with no history or safety data.[1]
Published research on EHT is mostly analytical, environmental and formulation work. No clinical trial of ethylhexyl triazone alone was found.
infobox: Not an approved sunscreen active (per Grokipedia)

paras: Ethylhexyl triazone has the formula C48H66N6O6 and a molar mass of 823.07 g/mol, with CAS number 88122-99-0 [1]. Wikipedia classifies it as a triazine, an aromatic amine and a 4-aminobenzoate ester, and gives its absorption maximum as 314 nm [1].

Grokipedia describes the molecule as a central 1,3,5-triazine ring with three anilino arms, each ending in a branched 2-ethylhexyl ester, which makes it oil-soluble and nearly insoluble in water; it appears as a white to pale yellow powder with a melting point near 129 degrees Celsius [2]. That account is AI-generated and has not been independently checked.

BASF markets the ingredient as Uvinul T 150, and DSM-Firmenich markets it as Parsol EHT [1]. Wikipedia lists it among sunscreen agents approved by one or more agencies [1]. Grokipedia states that it is permitted in the European Union under the Cosmetics Regulation at up to 5 percent, and that it is not an approved sunscreen active in the United States or Canada because the FDA's monograph process lacked data to classify it as generally recognised as safe and effective [2]. The same account says assessments such as one from Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration found low systemic absorption at approved levels [2].

EHT is used in sunscreens, creams, sprays and makeup, usually with other filters such as avobenzone.[2] A US drug label shows it combined with bisoctrizole, diethylhexyl butamido triazone and DHHB in one product.[3] Studies have examined organic filters in lipid nanoparticle formulations,[4] with ferulic acid to improve SPF and UVA protection factor,[5] and in tests comparing fifteen sunscreen products of equal label SPF under natural sunlight.[6]

Researchers have studied how filters photostabilise one another and quench triplet states in combination.[7] Percutaneous penetration of sunscreen filters has been measured in vitro with HPLC methods.[8]

A UK multicentre photopatch study of 1155 patients examined sunscreen chemicals as photoallergens, noting they are among the most common photoallergens in the UK.[9] A multi-centre European photopatch study is also registered.[10]

Filters of this type have been measured in wastewater and sewage sludge, with fate and removal studied across treatment plants,[11][12] in European sea sediment,[13] and in a toxicity test on brine shrimp and algae.[14]
No studies found for ethylhexyl triazone itself. Related human research covers sunscreens and photoallergens as a group.[9][10]

card.summary: A highly photostable UVB filter used in high-SPF products abroad; no clinical trials of it alone.
card.aka: Octyl triazone, EHT, Uvinul T 150, Parsol EHT
card.note: Not an approved US sunscreen active, per Grokipedia.

quick.overview:
Ethylhexyl triazone is an oil-soluble sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB light. It is used in products in the EU and elsewhere to help reach high SPF values.

Sources are thin: no clinical trials of it alone were found.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB near 314 nm and dissipates the energy as heat; it is typically combined with UVA filters.
quick.risks: Sunscreen filters as a class are recognised photoallergens in dermatology clinics. Environmental studies have measured similar filters in wastewater, sludge and sediment.

chain: Absorbs UVB light in a sunscreen or daytime cosmetic
Less UV exposure to skin, supporting even tone and slower photoaging
angle.text: Ethylhexyl triazone is an ingredient inside sunscreens and daytime cosmetics rather than a product people choose on its own. It raises the UVB protection of a formula, which supports the sun-protection habit people use to keep their skin looking even and youthful [2].
